indicators.note: 'in' drops what has just been named inside the word that follows, so the two letters sit within the hole rather than beside it.

blocks.note: a recess is a hollow cut back into a wall, a hole in it
standard abbreviation, as on a chess scoresheet
standard abbreviation, the L of a stage direction

explanation.surface: A rash monarch who has been left stuck down a hole.
explanation.walkthrough: 'King' and 'left' are two of the commonest single letters in the language of crosswords, and here they sit side by side. A recess is a hole in a wall rather than one in the ground.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe acting without weighing the danger, foolhardy leaning on the folly and reckless on the not caring.

indicators.note: To go around a thing is to close on the outside of it, so the grass wraps the word that follows instead of standing next to it.

blocks.note: a reed is a tall grass of the riverbank
a firm parent is a strict one

explanation.surface: A company's grounds with the boundaries of the grass marked out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grass' is the plant, not the police informer a setter usually means by it, and 'firm' is the adjective rather than the company the surface offers. Both have to turn over at once.
explanation.definitionFit: Ground that is restricted has a line drawn round where you may go, which is what demarcating it does.

indicators.note: A strange thing is not as it should be, so the letters beside it will not stay in the order they were given.

blocks.note: ten letters of fodder, the two words taken as they stand

explanation.surface: Taking back possession of one odd old rite.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strange' sits exactly where an adjective describing the ritual would sit, which is what hides it. 'Ritual' is a noun here and so is the answer: a ceremonial is the set order an occasion follows.
explanation.definitionFit: A ceremonial is the fixed form a rite is performed in, which is what ritual names when used as a noun.

indicators.note: To clutch a thing is to hold it fast inside your grip, so the answer is held unbroken inside the words before it.

blocks.note: the run begins on the fourth letter of the first word and stops one letter into the second

explanation.surface: Lying down with nothing on, hanging on to the bedclothes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Naked' reads as an instruction to strip a word of its outer letters, and is part of the hiding place instead. Bed linen is the shop's word for sheets and pillowcases sold together.
explanation.definitionFit: Bed linen is sheets and their like, so 'sheets' names the answer by the item most people buy under it.

blocks.note: a committee that assembled sat
one = I, and the 's supplies the S
a camp is a faction: the two camps in an argument

explanation.surface: Putting up somebody's tent so that the night will be comfortable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Camp' is the piece to see: not canvas but the group who take one side, as in the Leave camp. 'Assembled' is a court or a committee sitting, rather than anything being built.
explanation.definitionFit: Both name the contentment of a thing turning out right: you take satisfaction, or comfort, in work well done.

indicators.note: A reflex angle or a reflex muscle is one bent back on itself, so the word beside it is read from its last letter to its first.

blocks.note: used literally
a tress is a lock of hair

explanation.surface: A spring-loaded lock that snaps back of its own accord.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lock' is hair, not hardware, and 'maintain' is the courtroom sense: to assert a thing is to keep maintaining that it is so. 'Reflex' meaning bent back is rarer than the knee-jerk noun.
explanation.definitionFit: To maintain a position is to keep insisting on it, which is what asserting it amounts to.

clue.text: Go in street getting small prize for optimal location (5,4)

indicators.note: 'in' puts what has just been named inside the word that follows, so the go lands within the street.

blocks.note: standard abbreviation, the one on any British street sign
to go, in the nursery sense, is to have a wee — British children are told to go before a journey
standard abbreviation, the size on a clothing label
the pot is the prize money staked on a competition or a hand of cards

explanation.surface: Taking a turn along the street and picking up a small prize.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Go' is the nursery euphemism, and until you hear it that way nothing else lines up. A pot is the money a contest is played for, which is how one word of prize becomes three letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The sweet spot is the point on a bat or racket where the ball comes off best, and by extension any ideal place to be.

indicators.note: In a down entry 'up' points back towards the top of the grid, so the word before it is read upwards, last letter first.

blocks.note: to live is to be, in the sense of existing

explanation.surface: Somebody plainly up to no good.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue is a single idiom that already means what the answer means, so no word in it stands out as an instruction. LIVE turned round is a setter's favourite: a word that becomes its own opposite.
explanation.definitionFit: No good, said of a person or a deed, is the plain way of calling it evil without the biblical weight.

blocks.note: T is Tango in the NATO alphabet
a hen is a bird, the female of the domestic fowl

explanation.surface: A tango danced with a woman later in the evening.
explanation.walkthrough: The NATO alphabet is standing equipment for a setter: Tango is T, and Oscar, Victor and Mike are letters too. 'Bird' is the fowl here, not the dated slang for a girl.
explanation.definitionFit: Then means at that later moment — we ate, then left — which is what afterward says.

indicators.note: An eccentric wheel is one off its proper centre, so the letters beside the word will not stay where they were put.

blocks.note: eight letters of fodder, the two words taken as they stand

explanation.surface: A strange little fortune-teller taking everything calmly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cool' is the noun, the composure you keep or lose, not the adjective the surface wants for the seer. An indicator at the head of a clue passes as a description of the person.
explanation.definitionFit: Cool as a noun is the composure you keep or lose, and serenity is the settled form of it.

clue.text: Returned Little Life declaring parts dirty (6)

indicators.note: Something returned comes back the way it went, so the run of letters is read from its last letter to its first.
Parts of a thing are pieces of it rather than the whole, so what is wanted is a stretch of letters lying inside the words, not the words themselves.

blocks.note: the run starts on the last letter of the first word, takes the whole of the second and stops one letter into the third

explanation.surface: A returned copy of Little Life being declared dirty in parts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Returned' does the turning while reading as a book sent back to the shop, and 'parts' quietly says the letters are already lying in the clue. The capitals on Little Life are the disguise.
explanation.definitionFit: To defile something is to make it dirty in the strong sense, used of a stream, a shrine or a reputation.

indicators.note: To play with a thing is to move it about at will, so the letters named beside it come out in a new arrangement.

blocks.note: twelve letters of fodder, the two words taken as they stand

explanation.surface: A devil who has been told off and is now messing about.
explanation.walkthrough: Second fiddle is the player who follows the leader in an orchestra, which is why 'playing' beside it feels so innocent. Twelve letters of fodder in two ordinary words is the hardest kind to count.
explanation.definitionFit: To play second fiddle is to take the lesser part while somebody else leads, an orchestral seat turned into the idiom for any subordinate role.

indicators.note: A lining sits inside the thing it lines, so the skirts go within the word beside them rather than after it.

blocks.note: fresh news is recent news
minis are miniskirts

explanation.surface: A racy short skirt run up with a new lining.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Skirts' looks like the verb, to skirt round a thing, and is the garment in its short form. Reminiscent of and suggestive of are the same phrase: one thing calling another to mind.
explanation.definitionFit: A smell reminiscent of the seaside hints at it without being it, which is the sense 'suggestive' carries here.

blocks.note: Com. is the written short form of Commander, as it appears on a naval list
a passion for a subject is enthusiasm for it

explanation.surface: Taking pity on an officer who has rather too much enthusiasm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pity' opens the clue as a verb aimed at the commander and is the noun the answer matches. COM is the half nobody sees first, because commander looks like a whole word's worth of letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Compassion is fellow feeling for someone suffering, which is what pity names when it is kindly rather than condescending.

clue.text: Moron tears up seeing Galileo perhaps (10)

indicators.note: Tearing something up, or mixing it up, leaves it in pieces and out of order, so the letters before it do not stay as they were given.

blocks.note: ten letters of fodder, the two words taken as they stand

explanation.surface: An idiot in tears at the sight of Galileo.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tears up' reads as one phrase and splits in two: the tears are raw material and only 'up' does the scrambling. Galileo is one instance of the answer, which the 'perhaps' admits.
explanation.definitionFit: Galileo turned the new telescope on Jupiter's moons, so he stands as an example of the answer rather than a synonym for it.

clue.text: Boat made from bamboo perhaps with hole in (5)

indicators.note: 'in' puts the letter just named inside the word before it, so the hole sits within the cane.

blocks.note: bamboo is a cane, so the example hands over the general word
a hole is drawn as a round O

explanation.surface: A boat built out of bamboo, with a hole in it.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a leaky bamboo boat, near enough a real canoe that nothing jars. 'Perhaps' is the standing signal that bamboo is one kind of cane and not the word wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: A canoe is a light open boat driven by a paddle, so 'boat' is simply the class it belongs to.

clue.text: Kit starting to enjoy joke with blokes ahead of time (9)

indicators.note: The start of a word is where it begins, so only the opening letter of the word that follows is taken.
What is ahead of a thing comes before it, so the blokes are placed in front of the time rather than after it.

blocks.note: the first letter of enjoy
a quip is a joke made on the spot
bloke is British slang for a man
standard abbreviation, the t of any physics formula

explanation.surface: Beginning to enjoy a joke with the lads before it is time to go.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kit' at the head of the clue looks like a man being named — Kit Marlowe, say — and is the definition. T for time is the physics symbol, reached for whenever one letter of time is wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: Kit is the British word for the gear a job or a sport needs, which is what equipment names more formally.

clue.text: Shapeless, empty plinth held by Randy (9)

indicators.note: An empty thing has had its inside taken out, so the word keeps only the letters at its two ends.
What holds a thing closes round it, so the word that follows goes outside the letters just taken.

blocks.note: someone randy is amorous
the two ends of PLINTH, left when the middle goes

explanation.surface: A shapeless empty plinth being held up by a man called Randy.
explanation.walkthrough: Randy is capitalised to pass as a man's name and is the adjective, which is an easy switch to miss at the end of a clue. Emptying a word leaves its first and last letters standing.
explanation.definitionFit: Something amorphous has no definite shape of its own, which is what shapeless says of a cloud or a heap.

clue.text: Emptied bowels of European vessel holding a copper edition? (9)

definitions.note: Evacuated is used of the patient rather than the bowels, so the definition carries an object that the answer swallows; the question mark admits the stretch.

indicators.note: To hold a thing is to keep it inside, so what follows goes within the vessel's letters.

blocks.note: standard abbreviation, the E of E-numbers and EU paperwork
a vat is a vessel, the brewer's rather than the sailor's
used literally
Cu is copper's chemical symbol, from cuprum
standard abbreviation, as in 2nd ed.

explanation.surface: The hold of a European ship being cleared out, copper-bound edition and all.
explanation.walkthrough: A vessel is a vat as often as a ship, and 'bowels' is the hold of the one and the insides of the other. Cu for copper comes from cuprum, the Latin the chemists kept.
explanation.definitionFit: To evacuate, in the clinical sense, is to empty the bowels — the same verb used of clearing people out of a building.

indicators.note: Something done regularly happens at even intervals, so letters are taken from the word at a fixed step instead of all of them.

blocks.note: faucet is the American word for a tap
the even letters of h-E-a-R-d

explanation.surface: Water spilling from a tap you can hear dripping at steady intervals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heard' sits where a homophone signal belongs and is the word being sampled instead, every second letter. A spill is the twist of paper or thin wood you carry a flame on.
explanation.definitionFit: A spill and a taper are the same thing: the slender length of wood or waxed paper that takes fire from the hearth to the candle.

clue.text: Wandering relative returned from a gold prison in disarray (8,3)

indicators.note: A thing in disarray has been knocked out of its proper order, so the letters beside it are laid out afresh.

blocks.note: eleven letters of fodder, the three words taken as they stand

explanation.surface: A relative coming home from a gilded foreign gaol that has fallen into chaos.
explanation.walkthrough: The parable does the defining: the younger son goes off, spends the lot and comes back to the fatted calf. 'Returned from' belongs to that story and joins the halves without adding a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The son of the parable wanders off and squanders his inheritance before coming home, so 'wandering relative' describes him rather than translating him.

clue.text: Heads of agriculture believe animal care incentives to be things that can be counted on (5)

definitions.text: things that can be counted on

indicators.note: The head of a word is the letter it starts with, so only the opening letter of each word that follows is taken.

blocks.note: the first letters of the five words, in the order given

explanation.surface: Ministry chiefs deciding what to pay farmers for looking after their animals.
explanation.walkthrough: Counting on a thing normally means relying on it, and here it is meant literally. Five initials in a row is a long run, and the farming language keeps them reading as a sentence.
explanation.definitionFit: An abacus is a frame of sliding beads used for reckoning, so abaci are things you do your counting on, with the idiom pulling the other way.

clue.text: Gives weapons to ranches needing force (4)

indicators.note: A thing that needs something has not got it, so the letter named goes missing from the word beside it.

blocks.note: ranches are farms, the cattle sort
F is the symbol for force in any physics equation, and it is the letter that goes

explanation.surface: Handing out weapons to ranches that need some muscle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Needing' is the deletion word and it works backwards from how it reads: what is needed is what is not there. 'Arms' is the verb, not the noun the weapons invite.
explanation.definitionFit: To arm someone is to give them weapons, the verb sitting behind the noun everybody knows.

indicators.note: 'removed from' takes the piece just named out of the word that follows, leaving the rest standing in order.

blocks.note: a glaze is a finish: the glassy coat fired onto pottery
the leading letter of GLAZE

explanation.surface: A lazy leader being got rid of before the end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Idle' is the verb here — to laze an afternoon away — not the adjective the surface's leader invites. 'Leader' names a letter rather than a person, which is the other half of the switch.
explanation.definitionFit: To laze is to idle: to pass time doing nothing in particular, both working as verbs of a whole afternoon.

clue.text: Audience for book of French held by parent (6)

definitions.note: Audience names a whole body of people where the answer is one of them, but publishing habitually addresses that body in the singular as 'the reader'.

indicators.note: What holds a thing keeps it inside, so the French word sits within the parent's letters.

blocks.note: to rear a child is to parent it
de is the French for 'of', asked for by naming the language

explanation.surface: A parent holding a French storybook to read aloud.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Parent' is a verb here, which is what keeps REAR out of sight, and 'of French' is the standard way of asking for a French word rather than a French thing. DE is the commonest of them.
explanation.definitionFit: The people a book is written for are the ones who read it, so a reader is what its audience is made of.

clue.text: Impracticality of one trade is misunderstood initially (8)

indicators.note: Initially means at the very start, so only the opening letter of the word before it is used.

blocks.note: I = one, the Roman numeral
a trade is a deal struck
used literally
the first letter of misunderstood

explanation.surface: A single business deal whose impracticality nobody spotted at first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Is' does nothing but supply its own two letters, which is easy to miss in a word that reads as the sentence's verb. 'Initially' at the end reaches back over one word only, not the whole phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Idealism pursues things as they ought to be rather than as they are, which is why impracticality is the charge always laid against it.

indicators.note: Something disorganised has lost the order it was put in, so the letters beside it come out rearranged.

blocks.note: six letters of fodder

explanation.surface: The hustle of the street throwing a detective off his stride.
explanation.walkthrough: A six-letter first word beside a one-word definition is the shape an anagram usually takes. Sleuth comes from the sleuth-hound, the dog that follows a trail, and survives mainly in fiction.
explanation.definitionFit: A sleuth is a detective, named after the hound that follows a scent, and the word now belongs to storybooks and crosswords.

clue.text: Buck perhaps holding placard for architect (8)

indicators.note: To hold a thing is to keep it within, so the placard goes inside the animal's letters.

blocks.note: a buck is a male deer, so the example hands over the animal
a placard is a sign carried about

explanation.surface: A stag standing about holding up a protest placard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' warns that buck is one kind of deer and not the word itself, the same flag a setter raises over any example. Buck also passes as a man's name, which is the other trap.
explanation.definitionFit: An architect is the one who draws up the plan, and the designer of a dress, a chair or a policy does the same job.
